script: [serious] At seven fifty-five on the morning of December 7th, 1941, Japanese planes began bombing the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. In less than two hours, more than twenty-four hundred Americans were killed, and the United States was at war. But that morning, the attack had already been seen coming. Fifty-three minutes earlier, two young soldiers on a hilltop had watched the planes approach on a radar screen. An hour before that, a Navy destroyer had fired on an enemy submarine right at the harbor's entrance. Both warnings were reported. Neither one sounded the alarm. By the end of this file, you'll see exactly where each warning went, and why the one man everyone blamed may not have been to blame at all. In 1941, radar was brand new technology. The Army had set up several mobile radar stations around the island of Oahu to watch for incoming aircraft. One of them sat on a hill near the northern tip of the island, a place called Opana. Each station was a truck, a trailer, a generator and an antenna, run by a handful of young soldiers who were still learning how to use it. The radar could detect planes more than a hundred miles away. But it couldn't tell what kind of planes they were, or whose. Its reports went by telephone to a new information center at Fort Shafter, near Honolulu, where officers were supposed to plot them on a map and decide whether to send fighters up. That system was still being set up. Since a warning from Washington in late November, the radar stations had been running every morning, from four until seven a.m. After that, the soldiers could shut down and go to breakfast. The first warning came from the sea. Even earlier, at about a quarter to four in the morning, a minesweeper had reported seeing a periscope near the harbor. Then, just before six forty-five, the destroyer U.S.S. Ward, patrolling outside the entrance to Pearl Harbor, went after a small submarine trailing a supply ship toward the harbor. The Ward opened fire and dropped depth charges. It was the first American shot of the Pacific war, more than an hour before the attack. Its captain, Lieutenant William Outerbridge, radioed a report to naval headquarters. He reported that they had attacked, fired upon, and dropped depth charges upon a submarine operating in the defensive sea area. The message ran into busy phone lines and requests to confirm it. There had been false sightings of submarines before. The report moved slowly up the chain of command, officers asked for confirmation, and no general alert went out. By the time anyone acted on it, it was too late. Up at Opana, the radar crew was supposed to shut down at seven. But two privates, Joseph Lockard and George Elliott, decided to keep it running so Elliott could get more practice. At seven oh two a.m., a blip appeared on the screen. It was the biggest Lockard had ever seen. So big that at first he thought the machine was broken. It was about a hundred and thirty miles to the north, and getting closer. Elliott called the information center at Fort Shafter. Most of the staff had already left for the day. Elliott told the operator it was the largest group he had ever seen on the screen. The only officer there was Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, a fighter pilot who was on only his second day of duty at the center, with almost no training for the job. Tyler knew something the privates didn't. A flight of American B-17 bombers was due in from California that morning, coming from roughly the same direction. He told them, in effect, not to worry about it. Lockard and Elliott kept tracking the planes anyway, until they lost them in the hills near the island at about seven thirty-nine. Sixteen minutes later, the first bombs fell. The attack came in two waves. Japanese planes hit the battleships lined up along Ford Island, and the airfields around the island, where American planes had been parked wingtip to wingtip to protect them from sabotage. They made easy targets. The battleship U.S.S. Arizona exploded after a bomb hit its forward ammunition magazine. Eleven hundred and seventy-seven of its crew were killed. The Oklahoma capsized. The Nevada, the only battleship to get underway, was hit as it tried to escape the harbor, and had to be run aground. But some of the most important targets weren't there at all. The Pacific Fleet's aircraft carriers were away at sea that morning, and they survived. Japan lost twenty-nine planes. In all, more than twenty-four hundred Americans died, and nearly twelve hundred were wounded. And in the middle of the attack, the twelve B-17s that Tyler had been expecting really did arrive from California, unarmed and low on fuel, flying straight into the battle. The next day, President Roosevelt called December 7th a date which will live in infamy, and Congress declared war on Japan. In the weeks after the attack, the government searched for someone to blame. The top Navy and Army commanders in Hawaii, Admiral Husband Kimmel and General Walter Short, were relieved of command. A warning had been sent from Washington ten days earlier, telling commanders in the Pacific to expect possible Japanese aggression, and investigators said they had not done enough to prepare. That judgment is still argued over today. Both men spent the rest of their lives saying that Washington had withheld intelligence from them. Decades later, in 1999, the U.S. Senate passed a resolution saying they had been unfairly blamed, but it carried no legal force, and their ranks were never restored. Kermit Tyler was investigated too. An inquiry cleared him of wrongdoing. He had almost no training, no real staff, and the information center wasn't fully running. The radar couldn't tell friend from foe, and American bombers really were on the way. So here is what the file tells us. Pearl Harbor became the model for what investigators call a failure of warning. Not a lack of information, but a failure to connect it, and to act on it in time. Pearl Harbor wasn't a total surprise to everyone. A destroyer saw the danger. Two privates watched it on a screen. But the warnings went into a system that wasn't ready to believe them. If you had been the officer on that phone, what would you have done? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded.
